title: HelioSupport x Redwood — POC scoping (support agent + streaming)
next_steps: HelioSupport to share a 50–100 prompt set + expected outputs (or grading rubric) for agent responses
Redwood (Simran) to send recommended SDK integration pattern for streaming + retry semantics and a sample Node/Python snippet
Redwood to propose a rate-limit/concurrency plan for POC (initial caps + burst behavior) and confirm 429 handling guidance
HelioSupport to confirm target region(s) and whether VPC is required for POC or acceptable to start on Hosted
Schedule a 60-min technical working session to wire up streaming + fallback policies and review the evaluation harness
Avery to send a draft ‘reference call participation’ outline for HelioSupport review (frequency, topics, boundaries)
body:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: HelioSupport x Redwood — POC scoping (support agent + streaming)
Date: May 15, 2025
Time: 10:05am PT
Duration: 47 min
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
- Avery Johnson (Redwood Inference) — Account Executive
- Simran Kaur (Redwood Inference) — Solutions Architect
- Drew Patel (HelioSupport) — VP Support Ops
- Karen Li (HelioSupport) — Lead Platform Engineer
- Maya Sanchez (HelioSupport) — Product Manager, Agent Experience

Summary (auto-generated)
HelioSupport outlined a support-agent assistant use case with strict perceived-latency requirements and a strong preference for stable streaming in the UI. Redwood and HelioSupport aligned on POC scope: integrate streaming chat, implement fallback policies for model/region errors, and run a benchmark using a curated prompt set with latency + quality measurements. HelioSupport asked about handling 429s/timeouts, concurrency, and how Redwood recommends graceful degradation.

Key Topics
1) Latency targets and UX requirements for support agents
2) Streaming stability (SSE), disconnect/reconnect behavior, and timeouts
3) Fallback policies: model variants, region failover, and non-stream fallback
4) Rate limits, concurrency, burst behavior, and error handling
5) POC measurement plan: p50/p95 latency, first-token time, success rate, and quality evals
6) Reference call expectations (not a public case study yet)

Action Items
- HelioSupport: Provide sample traffic shape (req/s, concurrency, token lengths) and top 3 workflow types (draft reply, summarize case, internal KB answer)
- HelioSupport: Deliver prompt set + acceptance criteria by early next week
- Redwood (Simran): Share streaming guidance (keep-alives, reconnect, client timeouts) + recommended retry/backoff table
- Redwood (Simran): Draft a fallback policy config recommendation for HelioSupport (model + region + non-stream)
- Redwood (Avery): Send POC plan email with milestones, success metrics, and reference call boundaries

Transcript

[00:00] Avery Johnson: Cool, thanks everyone for making time. This is Avery at Redwood. Simran’s on as well. Goal today is to scope the POC so it’s super crisp—what you’re testing, what “pass” means, and what we need from each other.

[00:14] Drew Patel: Yep, sounds good.

[00:16] Karen Li: Yep.

[00:17] Maya Sanchez: Hi.

[00:19] Avery Johnson: Great. Maybe quick round of context from you all—what are you trying to ship and what’s driving the urgency?

[00:27] Drew Patel: So we’re building what we call “Agent Copilot” inside our support console. The agent is chatting with the customer, and the copilot suggests replies, summarizes the thread, pulls policy snippets. The biggest thing is it can’t feel slow. If it spins for like five seconds, agents just don’t use it.

[00:49] Avery Johnson: Makes sense. When you say slow—do you have specific numbers you’re targeting?

[00:54] Drew Patel: For streaming, we care about time to first token. Like, if it starts “typing” quickly, they tolerate the rest. If it just sits there, they don’t.

[01:04] Karen Li: Yeah. Internally we wrote down: first token under 500 milliseconds would be ideal. Under a second is acceptable. And then for typical suggestions—like 150 to 250 tokens—p95 end-to-end under, call it 2.5 seconds.

[01:23] Simran Kaur: That’s helpful. Just to confirm, that end-to-end is from you hitting “Generate” in the console to last token received?

[01:30] Karen Li: Correct.

[01:31] Simran Kaur: And you’re using SSE today?

[01:34] Karen Li: We use server-sent events, yes. We tried websockets. SSE was less finicky behind corporate proxies.

[01:41] Simran Kaur: Totally. SSE tends to be the least painful.

[01:44] Avery Johnson: And what’s your current stack? Are you calling OpenAI direct, or via Bedrock, or…?

[01:50] Maya Sanchez: Right now it’s a mix. For production we use OpenAI for a couple of flows, and we have an Anthropic one for longer summaries. We also started a Bedrock POC because procurement likes AWS. It’s messy.

[02:05] Drew Patel: Also cost is… not great.

[02:07] Avery Johnson: Understood.

[02:08] Simran Kaur: When you say streaming stability, what are the failure modes you’ve seen? Disconnects, partial responses, timeouts?

[02:16] Karen Li: All three. The worst is: we get tokens for a bit, then the connection drops, and the UI doesn’t know if it should retry, or if the model is still running and we’ll double-bill. So we’re trying to make it deterministic.

[02:33] Simran Kaur: Yep, that’s a classic. We usually recommend: client-side detect “no tokens for X seconds” vs “SSE disconnected”, plus a request id you can safely resume or reissue. We can walk through what we support.

[02:46] Avery Johnson: Maybe we should structure this as (1) what to test, (2) success criteria, (3) integration + ops, (4) reference expectations. Sound good?

[02:54] Drew Patel: Works.

[02:55] Maya Sanchez: Yep.

[02:57] Avery Johnson: Ok, (1) what to test. Our assumption is: you’ll integrate Redwood chat streaming into your agent console for 2–3 flows. Which flows matter most?

[03:07] Maya Sanchez: Draft reply is number one. Then summarize the ticket thread. Third is “suggest internal knowledge base answer” with citations.

[03:17] Simran Kaur: For the KB with citations, are you doing retrieval yourselves and passing context in? Or are you expecting the model endpoint to do that?

[03:24] Karen Li: We do retrieval. We pass in like top 5 chunks plus the ticket text. So prompt can be large. Sometimes 8k to 12k tokens input.

[03:35] Simran Kaur: Got it, that will affect latency. For the POC, do you want to include that long-context case, or focus on the shorter “draft reply” first?

[03:44] Drew Patel: If we can do both, great. But we’d rather have one flow that’s rock solid than three that are flaky.

[03:51] Avery Johnson: Makes sense. We can scope Phase 1 as “draft reply + streaming reliability”, Phase 2 as “long-context summarize + KB answer” if Phase 1 looks good.

[04:03] Karen Li: That’s fine.

[04:04] Simran Kaur: Cool. (2) Success criteria. You already gave two: time to first token < 1s p95, ideal 500ms; end-to-end p95 < 2.5s for 150–250 output tokens. Any other hard constraints? Like error rate.

[04:20] Karen Li: Error rate is huge. Like, we can’t have it fail more than 0.5%? I mean, during business hours. Also we need predictable behavior on 429. Today, some providers just… it’s not consistent.

[04:34] Drew Patel: Yeah, agents see “something went wrong” and they stop trusting it.

[04:37] Simran Kaur: When you say predictable, do you want a fast failure and then fallback? Or do you want to queue?

[04:43] Karen Li: For interactive, we prefer fast failure plus fallback. If the fallback is slightly worse quality, that’s fine.

[04:50] Simran Kaur: Perfect segue to (3) fallback policies. Redwood supports routing policies where you can define: primary model, secondary model, and optionally region fallback. Also a “streaming required” flag. If streaming can’t be established, you can switch to non-stream response with a timeout.

[05:10] Maya Sanchez: Can you do like—if primary model is overloaded, go to a smaller model but keep structure? Like tool calling.

[05:16] Simran Kaur: Yes, as long as the fallback model supports the same features—function calling / structured output. We’ll propose a compatible pair. Sometimes the names differ. Also, just to call it out, transcription might pick this up weird—KV cache, not “cash.” But anyway.

[05:30] Karen Li: (laughs) KV cash.

[05:32] Avery Johnson: It’s expensive cash, so fair.

[05:35] Simran Kaur: For your use case, the fallback policy we usually see is:
- Primary: highest-quality model that meets latency
- Secondary: lower-latency model with similar instruction tuning
- Region fallback: same model in another region if the first region has an incident
- If streaming errors: retry once quickly, then fall back to non-stream with a tighter max tokens

[06:01] Karen Li: We’d want to cap retries. Our UI team hates spinners.

[06:05] Simran Kaur: Yep. We can give you a table like: on network disconnect retry once with jitter, on 429 backoff 200–400ms and then fallback, on 5xx immediate fallback. Obviously we tune.

[06:19] Avery Johnson: Also, we should define your traffic shape for the POC. What’s peak concurrency when agents are in there?

[06:27] Drew Patel: Today we have about 600 concurrent agents at peak. Not all generating at once. But maybe 30 to 60 concurrent generations in the busiest times.

[06:38] Karen Li: For POC we can simulate 10, then 25, then 50 concurrency.

[06:44] Simran Kaur: Great. If you can share rough distribution for input tokens and output tokens per flow, we can pre-tune batching and timeouts.

[06:54] Karen Li: Yeah, we can pull logs. We’ll anonymize.

[06:57] Avery Johnson: Thank you. On rate limits: for the POC we can set a concurrency cap and a tokens-per-minute ceiling. We just want to align so you don’t hit a wall and think it’s “performance.”

[07:10] Karen Li: Totally. We’ve been burned by that.

[07:12] Maya Sanchez: One question: can you guarantee no partial responses? Like, if it fails, we’d rather have a clean error and a fallback answer.

[07:20] Simran Kaur: For streaming, there’s always a possibility of partial tokens delivered before a disconnect. What we recommend is: treat partial as “draft”, and only commit to the UI when you get an end-of-stream signal. If it disconnects mid-way, you show “retrying…” and then fallback. We can help implement that.

[07:41] Karen Li: That’s exactly the issue. Good.

[07:44] Avery Johnson: Ok, measurement. How do you want to validate p50/p95? Do you have existing harness?

[07:50] Karen Li: We have a little k6 script and some internal replay harness. But streaming metrics are tricky.

[07:56] Simran Kaur: For streaming we usually measure:
- TTFB / time to first token
- Token cadence (tokens/sec) or “gap time” distribution
- End-to-end latency
- Completion rate (did we receive end-of-stream)
We can provide a sample collector in Node that records timestamps per chunk.

[08:19] Maya Sanchez: We also want quality. Not just speed.

[08:22] Avery Johnson: Totally. Do you have a rubric? Like “agent accepted”, “agent edited”, etc.?

[08:27] Drew Patel: We do. Ultimately we want acceptance rate. But for POC we can do human grading on, say, 100 examples.

[08:36] Simran Kaur: Great. If you can give us 50–100 representative prompts, we can run them through a couple candidate models and compare.

[08:44] Karen Li: We’ll do that.

[08:46] Avery Johnson: (4) Reference call expectations. This is optional but it’s part of how we work with design partners. Would you be open to doing reference calls for other prospects if this goes well?

[08:57] Drew Patel: Maybe. I’m open, but I have constraints. We can’t do weekly calls.

[09:02] Maya Sanchez: And we’re not ready for a public case study. Maybe later.

[09:06] Avery Johnson: That’s totally fine. Many customers start “reference-call-only.” Typically we ask for 1 call per quarter, or 1 per month max, and we always prep you with the prospect context and topics to avoid. We can formalize boundaries.

[09:21] Karen Li: We’d also want to avoid specifics around our customer data, obviously.

[09:26] Simran Kaur: Of course. For reference calls, we can keep it to high-level outcomes: “improved streaming stability,” “met latency targets,” “fallback made it reliable,” without exposing internals.

[09:38] Drew Patel: That’s fine.

[09:40] Avery Johnson: Cool. Let me go back to deployment mode. Are you ok starting with Hosted API for the POC, or do you need VPC right away?

[09:49] Karen Li: We don’t need VPC day one. But we will eventually. Procurement and security will ask.

[09:55] Drew Patel: Yeah, we’re a support vendor, so our customers ask.

[09:58] Simran Kaur: Understood. For POC, Hosted is fastest. We can still set you up with SSO for console later. For security we can provide SOC 2 and data handling docs. But we can keep this POC focused on performance + UX.

[10:14] Karen Li: Perfect.

[10:16] Avery Johnson: Great. Let’s get more concrete on timeline. When do you want this live for internal testing?

[10:22] Maya Sanchez: Ideally two weeks to have something the agents can try.

[10:27] Karen Li: Engineering-wise, we can integrate in a week if SDK is clean.

[10:31] Simran Kaur: It’s pretty straightforward. We have a REST endpoint plus SDKs. Streaming is standard SSE. One thing: you’ll want to configure client timeouts carefully. Some libraries default to 30 seconds and then cut the stream.

[10:46] Karen Li: Yep, we hit that.

[10:48] Simran Kaur: We recommend:
- Keep-alive comment frames every ~10–15 seconds (if your infra allows)
- Client idle timeout > max generation time
- Server timeout aligned to max tokens
We can share defaults.

[11:06] Avery Johnson: And about max tokens—what’s typical output length for draft reply?

[11:12] Drew Patel: 120 tokens maybe. Sometimes 300.

[11:15] Maya Sanchez: We also want it to stop rambling.

[11:17] Simran Kaur: We can enforce max tokens and stop sequences. Also if you’re using structured output, you can bound it.

[11:25] Karen Li: Are you able to do JSON output reliably? Some providers say they do and it’s not.

[11:31] Simran Kaur: Yes. We support structured output and function/tool calling patterns. For POC we can start with “best effort JSON” and then tighten with a schema approach. But the more strict, sometimes the more latency. We’ll balance.

[11:49] Avery Johnson: Can we talk through failure scenarios and your desired UX? Like if primary fails, how fast do you want fallback to appear?

[11:57] Drew Patel: Ideally under a second to switch. If the agent sees nothing for 3 seconds, they’ll click again and make it worse.

[12:06] Karen Li: So we’d do something like: start streaming. If no first token by 900ms, cancel and try fallback.

[12:14] Simran Kaur: That’s a reasonable policy. We can implement on your side (client cancels + retries) or via our routing layer. I’d suggest via our routing policy so you don’t have to maintain complex logic.

[12:28] Karen Li: That’s better.

[12:31] Avery Johnson: Cool. On the question of cost: for POC do you have a budget ceiling?

[12:37] Drew Patel: We can spend a few thousand. We just need to see directional improvements.

[12:42] Avery Johnson: Fine.

[12:43] Simran Kaur: For measurement window: I suggest we do two tracks:
A) Synthetic benchmark: 100 prompts x N runs, record p50/p95 for TTF token and end-to-end.
B) Limited production pilot: 10 agents, measure acceptance and error rate.

[13:02] Maya Sanchez: Yes, that works.

[13:05] Karen Li: For the pilot, we can log first token time client-side.

[13:08] Simran Kaur: Great. We also have Console metrics that show token-level latency breakdowns. We can correlate.

[13:16] Avery Johnson: Also, I want to be clear about what we can commit to for the POC. We can commit to the plan and to support, but not SLA. But we’ll target your numbers.

[13:28] Drew Patel: That’s fine.

[13:30] Karen Li: One concern: we had issues with provider “warm ups.” Like first request after idle is slow.

[13:36] Simran Kaur: Totally. Cold starts. For hosted, we usually keep pools warm, but there can be variance. For your POC, we can set a minimum warm capacity and send periodic keep-warm pings. Also continuous batching helps once traffic is there.

[13:53] Karen Li: Ok.

[13:55] Avery Johnson: Let’s talk about what you need from us in terms of docs and sample code. Simran can send a streaming integration guide, plus recommended retry/fallback table.

[14:06] Simran Kaur: Yep. And also: a “do/don’t” list for SSE clients. For example, don’t buffer chunks, and make sure proxies aren’t buffering. Sometimes Nginx buffers by default.

[14:18] Karen Li: Yeah, we’re behind Cloudflare.

[14:20] Simran Kaur: Cloudflare can buffer if not configured. We’ll include notes.

[14:26] Drew Patel: Sorry, I have to jump in 10, but keep going.

[14:29] Avery Johnson: No worries. Before you go, can we align on reference calls? Just a soft yes conditional on success?

[14:36] Drew Patel: Conditional yes. One per quarter, maybe. And we want the right to say no depending on who it is.

[14:44] Avery Johnson: Totally fair. We’ll treat it as opt-in each time.

[14:47] Drew Patel: Great. Thanks.

[14:50] (Drew Patel left the meeting)

[14:52] Avery Johnson: Ok, Karen, Maya—back to technical details. Any compliance constraints we should bake in now? Data retention, logging, etc.

[15:01] Karen Li: For POC, we can use anonymized tickets. But long term we’ll need to know what logs you store and for how long.

[15:09] Simran Kaur: Understood. For Hosted, we have configurable retention for request logs and we can provide audit logs at the org level. But we can keep it minimal for POC.

[15:19] Maya Sanchez: Another question: If streaming disconnects, can you “resume” the stream?

[15:24] Simran Kaur: Not true resume where it continues from token 37. Usually you reissue with the same prompt and a system instruction like “continue” but quality can drift. Better is: fallback to a shorter response or show a message. For POC, we’ll focus on avoiding disconnects and handling them gracefully.

[15:44] Karen Li: Ok.

[15:46] Avery Johnson: Competitor-wise, you mentioned OpenAI/Anthropic/Bedrock. Are you also looking at Together or others?

[15:52] Karen Li: Together yes, because we want open models. But streaming was inconsistent.

[15:58] Simran Kaur: Makes sense. We can show you how we handle backpressure and chunking.

[16:04] Avery Johnson: Ok. Let’s lock deliverables.

[16:07] Avery Johnson: From HelioSupport by next Tuesday: prompt set 50–100, plus a doc with your three flows and expected token ranges. And your traffic shape.

[16:17] Karen Li: Yep.

[16:18] Maya Sanchez: Yep.

[16:20] Avery Johnson: From Redwood by end of week: integration doc, streaming do/don’t, proposed model pair and fallback policy. And we’ll set up your account with a POC key.

[16:31] Simran Kaur: Also I’d like a 60-min working session with your engineer who owns the UI streaming client. We can debug live if needed.

[16:39] Karen Li: That’s me and one of my team, Alex. I’ll bring him.

[16:44] Avery Johnson: Great. I’ll send scheduling.

[16:47] Maya Sanchez: Can we also align on what metrics you’ll show in your console? Like, we want to export them.

[16:54] Simran Kaur: Yes, you can export. We can also provide a CSV. We’ll show p50/p95 latency, tokens, errors. If you want first token, we capture that too.

[17:06] Karen Li: Ok.

[17:08] Avery Johnson: Any other questions or concerns?

[17:11] Karen Li: Just one: If we hit rate limits, can we pre-negotiate a temporary bump during testing?

[17:17] Avery Johnson: Yes. We can set higher caps for a defined window, just tell us before you run the load test.

[17:25] Maya Sanchez: And pricing—do we need to sign anything for the POC?

[17:29] Avery Johnson: For the POC, no. If we move to dedicated capacity or private later, yes. But we’ll keep it simple for now.

[17:37] Simran Kaur: One more technical note: for fallback, you’ll want to decide whether to keep conversation state on your side. We recommend you do, so switching models is simpler. We can talk in the working session.

[17:49] Karen Li: We keep state already.

[17:52] Avery Johnson: Great. Then I think we’re good. I’ll recap in email with the milestone plan and next steps, plus the reference-call boundaries draft.

[18:01] Karen Li: Sounds good.

[18:02] Maya Sanchez: Thanks.

[18:04] Avery Johnson: Thanks everyone.

(Transcript ends)
